flagged.title: Bank of England, East India Company and the trade revolution
flagged.reason: The video presents incorrect dates for the Calico Acts (1690 and 1720 instead of 1700 and 1721) and falsely claims Parliament renewed the East India Company's monopoly in 1700 when Parliament actually broke it in 1698.

mark_affecting.quote: This direct pressure led to the Calico Acts of 1690 and 1720.
And by 1700, Parliament had officially renewed their royal monopoly on Asian trade.

flagged.title: Consumerism, coffee houses and political activism
flagged.reason: The video presents Mary Astell as an anti-slavery writer and places Olaudah Equiano within the 1688–c.1730 period, both of which would cause students to lose marks for citing incorrect or out-of-period evidence.

mark_affecting.quote: writers like Mary Astell started pointing out the glaring hypocrisy of it all, like how could a nation constantly celebrate its own liberty while actively enslaving others?
someone who truly embodies the wild contradictions of this whole era is Olaudah Equiano... his early life directly crossed paths with this exact same coffee-house world we've been talking about

flagged.title: Spitalfields: site introduction and Huguenot weavers
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims that the Huguenot community built Christ Church Spitalfields as a statement of their prosperity, when it was actually commissioned and funded by Parliament under the 1711 Act to assert the Anglican Church over foreign Protestants.

mark_affecting.quote: Building this incredible structure and actually converting to Anglicanism was a huge statement. It proved their prosperity
